questions.question: Can a primary key be NULL or duplicate? Justify.
questions.solution_html:
• A Primary Key cannot be NULL because it must uniquely identify a tuple, and it cannot
  • contain duplicates because that would prevent distinguishing between two different
  • records.
  • All matching rows from both tables.
questions.final_answer: All matching rows from both tables

questions.question: What is the role of a lock manager in concurrency control?
questions.solution_html:
• The Lock Manager is the DBMS component responsible for managing locks requested by
  • concurrent transactions, maintaining a lock table to track granted locks, and forcing
  • conflicting transactions to wait.

questions.question: / is it preferred over file-based data storage?
questions.solution_html:
• Analyze the purpose of DBMS in managing large amounts of data. Why is it preferred
  • over file-based data storage?
  • The purpose of a Database Management System (DBMS) is to provide an efficient and
  • reliable way to store, define, manipulate, and share a large collection of related data for

questions.question: Compare column family and graph data models of NoSQL databases. / Discuss about dirty read, nonrepeatable read and phantom problem in a
questions.solution_html:
• Compare column family and graph data models of NoSQL databases.
  • Column family
  • Data is organized into rows, where each row contains a key and a set of column families.
  • Columns are flexible and can be sparse (a row may not have all columns).
  • Use Cases-Time-series data, high-volume logging, real-time analytics, and applications
  • requiring extreme horizontal scaling and write-heavy operations.
  • Excellent horizontal scalability (sharding/distribution is by row key).
  • Graph Data Model
  • Data is structured as a network of Nodes (entities) and Edges (relationships) with
  • associated properties.
  • Use cases-Social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection, and any system
  • where relationships are as important as the data itself.
  • Scales well for large numbers of nodes and edges; performance depends heavily on the
  • complexity of the traversal.

questions.question: / transaction. Explain the concept of FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL with proper syntax
questions.solution_html:
• Dirty Read (Temporary Update Problem)
  • a. Occurs when: Transaction T1 reads a data item that has been modified by a
  • concurrent transaction T2 , but T2 has not yet committed.
  • b. Problem: If T2 later rolls back its changes, T1 has read a value that never
  • officially existed in the database, leading to inconsistent results.
  • Nonrepeatable Read
  • c. Occurs when: Transaction T1 reads the same data item twice. Between the two
  • reads, a different transaction T2 updates or deletes that specific item and commits.
  • d. Problem: T1 gets different values for the same item upon repeating its read
  • violating the transaction's isolation.
  • Phantom Problem (Phantom Read)
  • e. Occurs when: Transaction T1 executes a query (e.g., a SELECT with a WHERE
  • clause) that retrieves a set of rows. A different transaction T2 then inserts a new
  • row that satisfies T1 's WHERE clause and commits.
  • f. Problem: When T1 repeats the query, it sees a new, unexpected "phantom" row
  • changing the set of rows retrieved

questions.question: / of a set of functional dependencies.
questions.solution_html:
• With suitable steps and examples, explain how to compute the closure of a set of
  • functional dependencies.
  • Given a relation schema R, a set of functional dependencies F, and a set of attributes
  • X⊆R, the closure X+is defined as: The set of all attributes that are functionally
  • determined by X using the dependencies in F.
  • compute X+ by iteratively applying Armstrong’s Axioms (reflexivity
  • augmentation, transitivity) until no more attributes can be added (Value liberally)
